subject: Coloring Boxplot Outliers to Match Box Fill

messages.author: 24cd2253f4cae0aa
messages.subject: Coloring Boxplot Outliers to Match Box Fill
parts:
Good Afternoon:

Below is a small sample data frame and code to create a grouped
boxplot using ggplot2.

library(ggplot2)

testdf <- data.frame(y1 = rexp(30),sources = gl(3, 10,
lab=LETTERS[1:3]))
#Typically rexp() results in at least one outlier in one group
bp <- ggplot(testdf, aes(x = factor(sources), y = y1))
bp1<-bp + geom_boxplot(aes(fill = sources)) +
scale_fill_manual('Data Source', breaks = c('A', 'B', 'C'),
values = c('red','green','blue'),
labels = c('A', 'B', 'C'))+coord_flip()+xlab('X Label')+ylab('Y
Label')+
opts(title="Title")
bp1

When I created this plot for a presentation at work (three groups with
n between 60 and 475) the data contained two to five outliers per
group and they appeared on the plot as the familiar solid, filled
black circles. Surprisingly, to me anyway, I had many questions from
the small audience about what the small, filled black circles
represented. When I pointed out that these were the outliers, there
were more surprising questions such as: why aren't they represented in
the legend? Can you make this clear somehow?

My initial thought is to color the outliers to match the fill color in
the boxes but despite several searches for help to accomplish this I
have not found the direction I need. Is there a way to do this? I
imagine that there must be and that I am simply looking right by the
solution, but I would very much appreciate any assistance from more
experienced ggplot2 users.

Thanks very much,

Adam

   opts(title="Title")
bp1

When I created this plot for a presentation at work (three groups with
n between 60 and 475) the data contained two to five outliers per
group and they appeared on the plot as the familiar solid, filled
black circles. Surprisingly, to me anyway, I had many questions from
the small audience about what the small, filled black circles
represented. When I pointed out that these were the outliers, there
were more surprising questions such as: why aren't they represented in
the legend? Can you make this clear somehow?

I think the point of having separate glyphs to represent unusual values is, in itself, a clear representation of sorts. (You can always increase the point size of the outliers :) I don't see why there is a need to 'represent them in [a separate] legend', especially if you have multiple outliers per group. Potential outliers are indicated in statistical graphics to highlight their unusual nature relative to the set of observations, suggesting that further investigation of those points is warranted. One option is to produce text labels in the vicinity of the possible outliers on the graph, but that strategy works when there are only a few such points - otherwise, the labels become distracting. In your case, I would tend to reserve discussion for the text if a document were to be produced or a separate slide if a presentation were to be given, perhaps with some notice to that effect in the figure caption.

Look at it this way: the simplicity of the graphic made the outliers noticeable to the audience and sparked a round of questions. As far as I'm concerned, mission accomplished. Had you adorned the graphic with some of the things you asked about in your post, would anyone have asked about them?  Would a discussion that ended with a conclusion that those points were something to be concerned about have ensued?  That's actually a part of graphics design.

I believe in simple graphics, but simple is not to be confused with simplistic. Effective graphics requires careful thought with a keen sense of purpose. This is why studying the graphics systems in R (ggplot2, lattice, base and grid) is worth the time, because their respective authors have devoted a lot of time, energy and thought into developing elegant ways to communicate ideas with data through visualization. An important question to ask yourself in this case is: will adding textual input to this plot convey vital information, or is it essentially chart junk?

My initial thought is to color the outliers to match the fill color in
the boxes but despite several searches for help to accomplish this I
have not found the direction I need. Is there a way to do this? I
Look at the outlier.color argument of geom_boxplot() - you should be able to map a fill color to it (if I read the help page correctly - I've never really done it myself so caveat emptor).

imagine that there must be and that I am simply looking right by the
solution, but I would very much appreciate any assistance from more
experienced ggplot2 users.

Thanks very much,

Adam

HTH,
Dennis

Hi:

It appears I was hasty in suggesting that outlier.colour could be mapped in geom_boxplot() - it can only be set by default. However, since there are a few serious ggplot2 hackers on this list, if someone wants to dig into the geom_boxplot() code to allow the outlier.* parameters to be mapped, I suspect Adam would be grateful :)

Cheers,
Dennis
